--- title: "Conway's Blobs" jupyter: brainvomit execute: echo: false warning: false --- ![](/assets/images/blobsim/thronglets.jpg) Conway's Game of Life is a neat little experiment that exploded in popularity due to its simple rules and complex emergent behavior. Basically, Conway simulated a grid of cells that could either be alive or dead. Each cell's current state is a function of the states of its neighbors. To start, the fundamental rules are: - Any live cell with < 2 live neighbors dies (underpopulation). - Any live cell with 2 or 3 live neighbors lives on to the next generation. - Any live cell with > 3 live neighbors dies (overpopulation). - Any dead cell with = 3 live neighbors becomes a live cell (reproduction). From these simple rules, complex patterns and behaviors emerge over time, often in ways that are difficult to predict. You can go down a wikiPedia rabbit hole exploring all sorts of self-organizing structures that arise depending on the starting configuration and the specific rules applied, such as: puffers, spaceships, and blinkers. (gifs of puffers, spaceships, and blinkers) ## Design BlobSim takes Game of Life, a cellular automaton, and extends it in 2 ways: 1. State is described not as dead or alive, but as a continuous energy level, where 0 is dead. 2. The rules for state transitions are probabilistic rather than deterministic. The world is a toroidal grid. Each cell can hold one **blob** — a simple creature with at any given time, an energy state and a fixed metabolism. Time advances in discrete steps t. At each step, each blob is allowed 1 action, which could be moving, eating, reproducing, or resting. Blobs are taxonomized based on the engine controlling their behavior. For example, Greedy blobs always prioritizes the nearest food-source (maximizes exploitation of resources), whereas RandomWalkers move randomly among all valid direction (maximizes exploration.) Their relative survival rate and distribution emerges over time based on these behaviors and the environmental conditions. To start, the environment is kept simple: each cell contains a max amount of energy **E_max** that, when consumed, gets regenerated at a rate of **r** per time step. The grid wraps around at the edges (a blob walking off the right side reappears on the left). The simulation runs in the same fixed sequence at each time step: 1. observe: each blob checks the state of its neighboring cells and its own internal state 2. decide: engines choose an action based on neighboring and internal state 3. conflict resolution: since time steps are discrete, the ordering of actions must be resolved (ie when two blobs attempt to move to the same cell, who gets priority?) Often this is by random or based on energy level. 4. pre-execution: the energy ledger is updated, resolved actions are applied to the grid and the blobs, conservation laws are enforced/checked 5. execution: the actual blobs and environmental cells are updated according to the validated actions in the pre-execution step ## Universal laws A set of invariants about this world are asserted, to maintain a somewhat coherent and internally consistent universe: - **Conservation of energy.** At any moment, the energy held by currently living blobs, plus the energy left in the grid, plus the energy differential of every action taken, plus whatever the environment has added, equals what the world started with - **Reproduction and predation only transfers energy.** A new blob is created from its parents' energy; a predation transfers energy from the prey to the predator - **Determinism.** The same random seed reproduces the exact same run - **One blob per cell.** No two blobs ever occupy the same square ## Example A finite grid with no replenishment can only end one way — the blobs spread until they deplete all the energy in the world and die out: ![Two kinds of blob draw down a finite grid until none are left.](/assets/images/blobsim/sc1_decay_extinction.gif) One run's population and total energy over time: ::: {#cell-live-sim .cell execution_count=2} ::: {#live-sim .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The simulation starts with a population bloom — the grazers find food and grow ~10× in ~20 steps, consuming at a rate faster than what the grid can maintain. At that inflection, energy dips while population peaks (the two runs *out of phase*). Those swings damp out, and both quantities settle onto their steady state, where the population is at its carrying capacity. ## Benchmark runs/base cases For purpose of sanity checking, each base case below computes an expected state *analytically from the rules* and then we check that the simulation derives it within some tolerance. ### Predicted lifespan A lone blob can either act or rest. Since it can only act on what energy is available, it stops acting when it reaches the minimum energy required to keep moving. From there, unless the cell is replenished, its energy drains at the fixed metabolic rate it dies. Adding the expected length of both cases gives a closed form, $$E[\tau] \;=\; \frac{E_0 - B}{E[c]} \;+\; \frac{B}{M} \;+\; (\text{boundary correction}),$$ with starting energy $E_0$, resting cost $M$, average active cost $E[c]$, and the minimum energy $B$ below which moving is no longer possible. For the test parameters this predicts **≈ 186 steps**, and the simulation agrees. But one match could be luck, so I varied the starting energy and the movement cost across ten settings and compared each one's *predicted* lifespan to its *observed* mean. Every point lands on the $y = x$ line — the formula tracks the simulation across the whole range, not just at one spot: ![Observed mean lifespan vs. the closed-form prediction. Points along the y=x line means good callibration, and the run-to-run spread is small.](/assets/images/blobsim/bench_lifespan.png) ### Guaranteed extinction on a finite grid If the environment does not regenerate energy, then the world's total energy can only decrease over time. Starting at $E_0$ energy and a per-step metabolic cost $m$, every blob must die within $$T_\text{max} = \left\lceil E_0 / m \right\rceil$$ steps. Notice how reproduction can't save it, because offsprings are created from parents' reserves. $T_\text{max}=E_0/m$ is a **ceiling**: it's how long the energy lasts if every joule goes to the cheapest possible expenditure — the metabolic cost $m$ per step. A blob that only *rests* hits the ceiling precisely; a blob that also *moves* dies sooner. Sweeping $E_0$ and $m$, the resters die right on the line and the movers run below it: ![Observed extinction limit vs. the ceiling T = E₀/m](/assets/images/blobsim/bench_extinction_time.png) ![Left: total energy (blobs + grid) over eight runs. Reproduction rate redistributes energy but can't change the extinction point.](/assets/images/blobsim/bench_extinction.png) ### Carrying capacity If the environment replenishes energy, the population settles at a point where energy in = energy out -- a *carrying capacity*. The equivalence is written as: $$N^* \approx \frac{\text{rate}\times\text{cells}}{\text{rate} + \bar e},$$ where $\bar e$ is the energy cost per step. Plotting raw runs over time shows what equilibrium looks like. The population doesn't sit *at* the carrying capacity — it **oscillates** around it in boom-bust cycles. But a sparse start (10) and a dense start (300) both regress into the *same* oscillation pattern, centred on ≈ 133, within ~20 steps: ![Raw population over time. The sparse run starts at 10 and the dense run at 300 (dots); both boom immediately, then settle into the same boom-bust oscillation around the carrying capacity ≈ 133 — regardless of their initial state.](/assets/images/blobsim/bench_carrying_time.png) The empirical carrying capacity is **~133**, which is ~20% below what we predicted. Why?? The unaccounted factor is local density: in a crowded space, blobs are more likely to idle than move. To improve our estimate of energy expenditure, measure what blobs *actually* spend — energy dissipated per step ÷ blobs alive — and it comes to $\bar e \approx 0.20$ (a move rate near **50%**). Plugging that into the equation gives **133**, matching the observed equilibrium. As you can see, the rulebook fixes the *costs* (metabolic 0.1, move 0.2) but not how blobs actually behave. $\bar e$ and $N^*$ co-determine each other in a closed loop: the only way to know $\bar e$ is to run the simulation, ie there is no closed form solution to this question. ### A lone blob's energy A single blob on a quickly-replenishing grid absorbs more each step than it spends, so its energy maxes out and then stays there: ![Energy of a single blob across several runs — each maxes out (at 60) within ~15 steps.](/assets/images/blobsim/bench_lone_energy.png) ### Extinction threshold Whether a population survives in the long run hinges on how fast the grid replenishes. There is a **critical rate**: below it, blobs can't absorb enough excess energy to produce at least 1 surviving offspring. Below this energy rate, the population dies out; above it, they persist. The crossover is like a phase transition: ::: {layout-ncol=2} ![Below the critical rate — the population dies out.](/assets/images/blobsim/c2_extinction.gif){width="320"} ![Above the critical rate — the population survives.](/assets/images/blobsim/c2_survival.gif){width="320"} ::: Sweeping the rate and measuring how often the population survives (10 seeds per rate) draws out the transition: survival jumps from near-zero to near-certain across a narrow band around the critical rate ≈ 0.075. ![Survival probability versus grid replenishment rate. The sharp rise across ~0.075 is the phase transition.](/assets/images/blobsim/bench_threshold.png) ### Grazers vs. walkers I decide to put 2 species in the same world and compare their relative survival rate: 1. **Random walkers** move randomly 2. **Grazers** move toward the neighbouring cell with the most energy With identical metabolism, the grazers on average, absorb more per step, so they reproduce faster and eventually take over. ![Energy-seeking grazers outcompete random walkers.](/assets/images/blobsim/c3_competition.gif) ## Emergent behavior I was interested in emergent patterns/behavior which are non-closed-form and can only be discovered through simulation. ### Predation A blob can **predate** an adjacent blob of a species it preys on. Hunt success is determined by energy: the predator eats only if it currently holds *more* energy than its prey; a failed hunt costs the minimum energy to make the attempt. Crucially, predators stay **omnivores**: every blob still grazes the grid as before; hunting is purely opportunistic. ### The ouroboros If you have a cycle of three species where A eats B, B eats C, and C eats A (rock, paper, scissors), no one is dominant, and from a random scatter the grid spontaneously sorts itself into travelling patches that chase each other forever (but only when the world is big enough.) Coexistence is a *spatial* effect: the three survive because the rotating patches keep them apart. Shrink the grid and any random extinction cascades — one species loses its only predator, booms, and wipes out the third — collapsing the cycle to a single colour. (Below a world < 20 cells wide it almost always collapses; past ~36 it reliably survives [below](#how-big-must-the-world-be).) ::: {layout-ncol=2} ![Big world (60×60): the three sort into rotating domains](/assets/images/blobsim/cyclic_ouroboros.gif){width="300"} ![Small world (18×18): a random fluctuation kills one species, the cascade fires, and only one colour survives.](/assets/images/blobsim/cyclic_collapse.gif){width="300"} ::: ![The cyclic world across the run ](/assets/images/blobsim/cyclic_frames.png) The population never converges: each population oscillates, peaking after the species it eats — measured, each colour lags the one it preys on by **~60 steps**, the same lag all the way round (A→B→C→A), which is exactly what a rotation looks like in time. Two views of that rotation — the populations over time (left), and the same whole-grid A:B:C mix drawn step by step as a path on a triangle (right), where each corner is "all one species", the centre an even split, and colour runs dark (start) → bright (end): ::: {layout-ncol=2} ![Populations over the run — sustained, out-of-phase oscillation; each peak chases the availability of prey.](/assets/images/blobsim/cyclic_populations.png) ![The whole-grid mix drawn as a path, orbiting the three-way centre — never reaching a corner or settling.](/assets/images/blobsim/cyclic_orbit.gif){width="240"} ::: The system never diverges into corners (no species ever wins) and never reaches the centre (convergence) — its population mix is in perpetual orbit. Can we predict the minimum grid size needed for coexistence? The prediction is that the minimum grid size is described by the **wavelength** $\lambda$ — the width of each rotating patch. I measured $\lambda$ independently, from the spatial autocorrelation of a single species on a large (70×70) grid: $\lambda \approx 33$ cells. Then I swept the grid size and measured how often all three survive: ![Survival vs. grid size (12–20 runs per point, more near the transition). Coexistence is near-impossible below ~20, turns on through the mid-20s, and is reliable past ~36. The independently-measured wavelength λ ≈ 33 (blue dashed) lands right where coexistence becomes reliable.](/assets/images/blobsim/cyclic_finite_size.png){width="460"} The agreement is there: $\lambda \approx 33$ sits on top of the transition, where survival becomes increasingly probable. Basically, the world has to be about ~one spiral wide for coexistence to be possible. **More than three?** ![A five-species cycle (72×72): A→B→C→D→E→A](/assets/images/blobsim/cyclic_five.gif){width="320"} ANYWAYS this was a fun project that was long and honestly ambiguously useful in any sort of way. But at least now you know what the people who were weirdly into fractals as children are up to nowadays. ## Gallery Further simulation runs not featured above, generated from the `blobsim` package. ::: {layout-ncol=4} ![Cyclic world — energy-sensing](/assets/images/blobsim/case_energy.gif) ![Cyclic world — blind omnivore](/assets/images/blobsim/case_blind.gif) ![Sensing — energy (≡ full: the extra info changes no decisions)](/assets/images/blobsim/sense_energy.gif) ![Asymmetric 3-cycle — one predator over-powered, still coexists](/assets/images/blobsim/asym_3.gif) :::
